messages.author: cc6f7d896cb5b9c9
messages.subject: Stuck on geolocation data format issue
parts:
Hello everyone,

I've just discovered the Distance software and I'm trying to learn how it works, particularly for determining transects. 

Unfortunately, I'm stuck at the very first step due to a data formatting issue when defining the study area. If I use the example data available in the software manual, in the "Study Area" section, and double-click on "polygon," then copy/paste the coordinates of the study area, I get an error message: "257 lines of input were not of the format 'number tab number' and so were treated as indicating separators between parts of multi-part shape." 

When I click OK, I can see there's an issue because the x and y coordinates are not entered, and instead I see ".....Separator....".

  I also tried using the coordinates for my own project with a .txt format, with the coordinates in DMS, but it was also unsuccessful...  

Can anyone help me with this? can you give me an example of data format that is accepted by the software ?

Thank you,

Océane

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Stuck on geolocation data format issue
parts:
Océane

Welcome to the list.  As with most things with the Distance for Windows software, we have tried to provide examples of its use and also provide multiple ways to accomplish most tasks.

I presume you are following the example in Chapter 3 of the users guide "Using Distance to Design a Survey".  As you note, there is a text file "StAndrewsBay.txt" located in the Sample Projects directory that you can use to bring coordinates into Distance for Windows. That text file contains sets of UTM coordinates separated by a tab.



Below, you will see a screen shot of a text editor containing that text file. I followed the users guide instructions, copied the coordinates from the text editor to the clipboard, then used the "Copy from clipboard" command in the data tab to bring those coordinates into the Study Area vertices.


If you have a shapefile containing the outline of your study area, you can use the Import Shape Wizard as the smoothest way to get geographic data into Distance for Windows.


By the way, degrees/minutes/seconds is probably not the best form for geographic data as degrees of latitude differ in size over the globe. Have a more thorough read of the users guide on the subject of projections and such.

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Stuck on geolocation data format issue
parts:
Just to augment what Eric said: Distance for Windows can also deal with
data in latitude and longitude, but it's easier for most people to do
the projections outside of Distance.

Here is some information about it, in case anyone wants to go this route:

If you want to import the data in latitude and longitude, it has to be
in decimal degrees, not degrees-minutes-seconds format. It's easy to
convert from one to another:

decimal degrees = degrees + minutes / 60 + seconds / 3600

Once this is done, you can readily import the data into Distance using
the copy/paste method. However, you then need to set a geographic
coordinate system for the layer (in Data layer properties, under the
Geographic data tab, click on Change coordinate system and then choose a
Geographic coordinate system from the drop-down), or (probably easier)
choose a default geographic coordinate system for the project before you
create any layers (File | Project Properties under the Geographic tab).
Also note that if you're doing survey design, you then need to define a
projection so that the design calculations can convert latitude and
longitude into x and y in meters for the purposes of creating designs.
(This is under design Properties, General Properties, Design Coordinate
System.)

More information about this is in the Users Guide, in Chapter 5 (Data in
Distance) under "Geographic (GIS) Data".

Hopefully this is useful. Cheers, Len
